newsitem.title: GERMANY: Field down to three for sale of Vulkan's STN Atlas.
newsitem.headline: Field down to three for sale of Vulkan's STN Atlas.

text.p: Talks on selling STN Atlas, the defence unit of stricken German shipyard group Bremer Vulkan, have entered their final stages and three bidders are now left in the race, companies involved said on Friday.

A local television station in the north German port city of Bremen reported that Germany's Mannesmann, Diehl and British Aerospace had made it onto a shortlist out of an original 30 bidders for STN Atlas.
Both Mannesmann and British Aerospace confirmed their interest in STN Atlas, but Diehl, a Nuremberg-based armaments company, declined to make any immediate comment.
A Mannesmann spokesman told Reuters the company was mainly interested in STN's defence technology business, and was also open to the possibility of a joint takeover bid.
"We are talking to everybody," the spokesman said, but gave no further details.
Klaus Rettig, who heads British Aerospace's German operations, told Reuters that BAe had put in an offer to take over STN Atlas completely.
"We want to keep the business as it is and turn it into a European defence systems company in land and marine operations," Rettig told Reuters.
Rettig also said he would welcome an alliance with other bidders as long as they shared similar strategic goals to BAe.

Bremer Vulkan receiver Jobst Wellensiek declined to comment on Friday, but has repeatedly stated that he wanted to complete the STN Atlas sale this year for at least 600 million marks ($393.6 million).

STN Atlas is the only profitable unit of Bremer Vulkan, which went bankrupt this year. It emerged that management had siphoned European Union subsidies earmarked for ex-Communist eastern Germany to prop up the group's shipyards in the west.
The Bremen Radio television channel said on Thursday that BAe had made a "financially interesting" offer, and company officials had been in Bremen this week to take a closer look at the company.
But Rettig told Reuters that the due diligence process was continuing and it was still too early to put an exact price tag on STN Atlas.
The defence ministry has in the past called for STN Atlas to be sold to a German buyer, but Wellensiek has said that would have no impact on his decision.
"The defence ministry is still uncompromisingly for a domestic solution," BAe's Rettig said. "But we have the best offer."

The fate of Bremer Vulkan's shipbuilding operations looks less promising, with the Bremen city senate on Friday rejecting calls by EU competition commissioner Karel Van Miert for capacity to be cut back in Bremerhaven and Bremen.
Van Miert said in a television interview that future EU subsidies to Bremer Vulkan's facilities in both east and west Germany would depend on further shipyard closures.
-- Douglas Busvine, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($ = 1.524 German Marks)
